genxml.title: VPro (Odyssey) display registers (publish-safe subset)
genxml.from: odsy binary analysis of the shipped display driver
genxml.doc: Display-half registers of the Odyssey board: colour map, line and frame tables, cursor, DAC, timing generator, genlock and the display-mode table.

struct.name: CMAP
struct.from: odsy binary analysis of the shipped display driver
struct.doc: Colour map. One entry per register, indexed by the entry number in the display FIFO header address. Each entry packs three 10-bit channels. The software widens an 8-bit input channel c to 10 bits as (c << 2) | (c >> 6), repeating the top two bits. The map has 8192 entries: the published diagnostic reference steps the red, green and blue index to 8191 and calls that the maximum size, and the line table begins where the map ends. No X visual declares more than 4096 entries. Bits 31:30 are never set by any shipped writer. The driver waits for the display FIFO to drain before a textport write; the X server path loads runs of entries as multi-word FIFO packets of the retrace-synchronised kind.

struct.name: LINE_TABLE
struct.from: odsy binary analysis of the shipped display driver
struct.doc: Video timing line table, up to 2048 16-bit entries, two per word with the even entry in the low half. A line type is a run of entries ending at the first entry with bit 15 set. For the timed entries bits 14:8 behave as a duration in pixel clocks (the first timed run of the built- in 1280 by 1024 timing is the horizontal sync width); this fails for some later line types, so it is a partial reading. The low byte of an entry is the output state for the span: which signal each bit drives is unknown. The loader zeroes the whole table (1024 words) before it sends a new one.

struct.name: FRAME_TABLE
struct.from: odsy binary analysis of the shipped display driver
struct.doc: Video timing frame table, up to 256 16-bit entries, two per word like the line table. Entries come in pairs: the position of a line type in the line table (in 32-bit words) and how many consecutive lines use it. The list ends with a (0, 0) pair. The counts of a timing add up to its total lines per frame. The loader zeroes 128 words before it sends a new table.

struct.name: VTG_CTL
struct.from: odsy binary analysis of the shipped display driver
struct.doc: Video timing generator control word. The loader writes the timing structure's control word with 0x42 ORed in, then writes 1 after the clock is programmed. The genlock handler clears and sets bit 1 here as the lock state changes (set while locked, inferred from the handler's two branches).

struct.name: VTG_INIT_STATE
struct.from: odsy binary analysis of the shipped display driver
struct.doc: Timing generator initial-state word. The driver reads it back once at start-up as its shadow and clears bit 5 of the shadow to blank the screen. The loader writes the timing structure's initial-state word here.

struct.name: VTG_CHAN_EN
struct.from: odsy binary analysis of the shipped display driver
struct.doc: Timing generator channel-enable word. Blanking clears the three bits of mask 0x23 (bits 5, 1 and 0) in the driver's shadow of it and unblanking sets them again; the timing load writes the structure's word with the driver's own bit 5 kept. The names are ours: what each bit gates is unknown.

struct.name: CURSOR_IMAGE_A
struct.from: odsy binary analysis of the shipped display driver
struct.doc: Cursor image block A, 128 words. A 32 by 32 cursor at 4 bits a pixel is 512 bytes, which is this block. Each pixel indexes the cursor colour table; index 15 has no entry and inverts the pixel under the cursor. The stored image is the bitmap with its two middle nibble columns swapped and mirrored. The shipped driver names this block the glyph plane and block B the alpha plane.

struct.name: CURSOR_POS
struct.from: odsy binary analysis of the shipped display driver
struct.doc: Cursor position word: the cursor x minus the hotspot x in the high half and y minus the hotspot y in the low half. The kernel sends it as a display-FIFO record of type 3 when bit 2 of the cursor control word is clear and type 7 when it is set (display.md, cursor). Whether a type 7 update takes effect at once or at the next frame is unknown.

struct.name: CURSOR_CTL
struct.from: odsy binary analysis of the shipped display driver
struct.doc:
Cursor control word, sent whole on every change. Start-up writes 0. The firmware textport clears bits 4:2 and sets bits 1:0 (established).
Software use per bit, from a reading of the shipped X server module and the kernel's display driver. That reading was not repeated for this entry, so the grades are the reading's own: - Bit 0: set in the word that shows the cursor and clear in the word that hides it, in both the X module and the kernel (usage established; that it is the display enable is inferred). - Bit 1: kept by software as a "shown" flag. Hardware meaning unknown. - Bit 2: set only for the X module's built-in crosshair cursor, and then the kernel tags its position records with header bit 30 (usage established; that it selects a hardware crosshair is inferred). - Bit 4: set when one X screen spans two display channels. Hardware meaning unknown. - Bit 5: marks the cursor on the second display channel (meaning inferred). The kernel sets it when it positions the cursor. - Bits 31:30: set by the firmware, never by the X module or the kernel. Hardware meaning unknown.
The field names below are an older guess. They put delay enable at bit 0 and enable at bit 1, which conflicts with the bit 0 usage above. Open questions records the conflict; the names stay until it is settled.

struct.name: CURSOR_COLORS
struct.from: odsy binary analysis of the shipped display driver
struct.doc: Cursor colour table, 15 words for pixel values 0 to 14, in the colour- map entry format. Software shifts an 8-bit value into the top eight bits of each 10-bit field, leaving the low two bits zero.

struct.name: CURSOR_IMAGE_B
struct.from: odsy binary analysis of the shipped display driver
struct.doc: Cursor image block B, 64 words: 2 bits a pixel, the alpha plane that decides where the cursor shows. Alpha 3 is an opaque cursor pixel and 0 transparent (inferred from the one shipped arrow image). Alpha 1 and 2 have no known fixed meaning.

struct.name: DATAPATH_CTL
struct.from: odsy binary analysis of the shipped display driver
struct.doc: Data-path control of the display chip. The timing load writes the structure's word here and sets bit 7 when bit 6 of that word is set. The blanking routine reads it back. The role is inferred from the order of the driver's stores; bit meanings beyond the two named are unknown.

struct.name: AUX_CTL
struct.from: odsy binary analysis of the shipped display driver
struct.doc: Written once per timing load from a word of the timing structure that sits next to the DAC and data-path words. What it controls is unknown.

struct.name: DAC_CTL
struct.from: odsy binary analysis of the shipped display driver
struct.doc: DAC control. Blanking sets bit 0; the DAC-gain routine sets or clears bit 1 with a read-modify-write; the timing load writes the structure's DAC word. That bit 0 blanks is established by the routine; the polarity of the gain bit is not known, so its name is inferred.

struct.name: VTG_MISC
struct.from: odsy binary analysis of the shipped display driver
struct.doc: Twelve consecutive timing generator words, written in order from twelve consecutive words of the timing structure. Bit meanings are unknown.

struct.name: GENLOCK_CTL
struct.from: odsy binary analysis of the shipped display driver
struct.doc: Genlock control. The timing load writes the structure's word here after enabling the genlock interrupt source, and the genlock handler continues only when bit 6 is set, which reads as a genlock-enabled flag (inferred). While the clock is being reprogrammed the word is held at 0.

struct.name: GENLOCK_STATUS
struct.from: odsy binary analysis of the shipped display driver
struct.doc: Genlock status, read only. The handler returns if bit 0 is clear. Bit 1 selects the branch that reprograms the clock part: set takes the "lost" branch, clear the "got" one. The handler's own message calls bit 0 the generator state; what bit 1 means beyond selecting the branch is unknown, so the name valid is a guess.

struct.name: MODE_TABLE
struct.from: odsy binary analysis of the shipped display driver
struct.doc: Display-mode table: one mode word per display id, ids 0 to 36 seen in the shipped tables (the upper bound is unknown). Type-7 (retrace- synchronised) FIFO writes. Ids below 32 are the window ids that double- buffer; bit 30 of the caller's mode is a software buffer flag the kernel strips before the write. For ids below 32 the colour-map group is bits 8:4, for ids from 32 up it is bits 7:3. Every colour-index mode seen has pixel_format 0, 3, 6 or 7 (not a channel width); across the TrueColor modes the codes below are established as values and their mapping to depth is inferred from which visual each table row serves. Colour-map group 26 appears on every TrueColor mode and is read as the gamma map. A published driver sets two bits among 31:25 (bits 31 and 28) in the one word it writes to all entries; no shipped mode word has either set and what they do is unknown.

struct.name: CMAP_UNIT_CTL
struct.from: odsy binary analysis of the shipped display driver
struct.doc: Colour-map unit configuration. Start-up writes 0; the timing load stores a flag bit of the timing load, the same flag it stores to the second scan configuration register in PBJ_DECODE.h.

struct.name: CMAP_OVERRIDE
struct.from: odsy binary analysis of the shipped display driver
struct.doc: Red, green and blue overrides of the colour-map unit, in that order. Start-up writes 0 to each.
